articles.title: Leveraging the solar revolution
articles.content: AT COP31, Prime Minister Shehbaz Shariftolda high-level dialogue on electrification that “an extraordinary transition has already taken place” in Pakistan: nearly 22 gigawatts of rooftop solar in two years, “a quiet revolution by ordinary citizens seeking affordable power and a cleaner, more predictable future”. More than one in 10 motorcycles sold this year, he added, was electric. He was right to showcase it. Few countries can match that speed. Fewer can accept that their citizens paid for it. Nobody planned it: capacity payments rose whether plants ran or not, the rupee fell, and the 2023 IMF programme stopped the state hiding these costs in subsidies. Base tariffs doubled between FY22 and FY25, just as Chinese panels became cheap and loadshedding persisted. The IMF did not create the high cost of power. It made it visible, and achieved the revolution by accident, what policy had not. The dividend is large. By the estimates of Ember, CREA and Renewables First, distributed solar avoided over $12 billion in oil and gas imports by February 2026, with $6.3bn more expected this year, and about 35 million tonnes of CO2 in FY25. Counting grid losses, it supplies about a third of the country’s electricity. On farms, solar runs 52pc of 1.83m irrigation pumps, almost entirely without state help. Banks financed less than 5pc of the $14bn invested. The official response has been to contain it, with a sales tax on panels andcuts to net metering. A showcase needs a strategy. The leveraging should run on two tracks. Phase one put panels on roofs; phase two must make that power go further. The first is phase two. Phase one put panels on roofs; phase two must make that power go further. Rooftops have already displaced most of the daytime thermal power they can reach, so more panels alone bring falling returns. Three areas will win the game. Storage, with a tariff that spreads the grid’s fixed costs fairly, so surplus daytime power serves the evening peak. Transport, where petrol imports are still growing: electric motorcycles reached 13pc of sales by August, already ahead of the New Energy Vehicles Policy’s schedule. The 30pc target should move from 2030 to 2028 for automobiles, two-wheelers, rickshaws and delivery fleets first, with battery-swap and charging corridors for bikes and freight planned along the motorways now. And solar mini-grids for the 40m people still without electricity. The prize is worth the effort. Adding 3GW of distributed solar a year would lift avoided emissions to about 50m tonnes by 2030, as per Renewables First estimates, more than the power sector now emits. At this year’s rate, fuel import savings by then would approach $25bn. Electric bikes save less, but their savings will help poorer households, which is where a transition survives or dies. The second track is harder. If fiscal conditionality could transform mitigation by accident, what could adaptation measures achieve by design, without waiting for grants or loans? Agriculture uses more than 93 per cent of the country’s freshwater, yet produces under $1 of output per cubic metre, against a global average near $17. Solar has made matters worse: once panels are paid for, pumping groundwater costs nothing at the margin. The rice area grew by about 30pc between 2023 and 2025, even as Punjab’s water tables fell. Flooded paddies also emit methane, so the same expansion that drains aquifers adds to emissions. Islamabad and the provinces already hold the levers. Five would do the most. First, conditional solarisation. Punjab already subsidises tubewell conversion; each should require drip or sprinkler irrigation and a flow meter. The Punjab Water Act 2019 allows new solar wells to be registered. Second, volumetric abiana. The canal water charge is so low that sugarcane and rice grow where the water cannot support them. Charging by volume and crop is a provincial power, and it raises revenue. Third, retargeted fertiliser support. IMF pressure ended most of the feedstock gas subsidy to urea plants in 2024. Blanket urea still invites overuse; the excess escapes as nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas, or leaches into groundwater. Tying the remaining support, including Kissan Card credit, to soil testing and slow-release coated urea would cut the waste and the fertiliser bill together. Fourth, alternate wetting and drying for rice. Letting paddies dry between irrigations cuts both water use and methane. Punjab and Sindh can initiate this through their extension services and Kissan/Hari cards, with a low-carbon basmati label for buyers who increasingly ask about embedded emissions. Fifth, a satellite-enforced no-burn rule. Tying Kissan Card eligibility and wheat procurement to satellite checks on residue burning, already run for smog, is an administrative change. Lahore would breathe cleaner air. None of these needs a donor. The petroleum levy brought in a record Rs1.57 trillion in FY26, and the climate support levy is budgeted at Rs50bn this year. Ring-fencing a fixed share of the first, and all of the second, would fund them without waiting on donor cycles. The provinces, which own agriculture and irrigation, ran a combined cash surplus of Rs1.45tn last year, led by Punjab; only Balochistan’s was marginal. Those surpluses are an IMF target, which brings the Fund back in. Its $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility already lists irrigation water pricing, but its water measures are hostage to influential interest groups. The two remaining reviews in 2027 can begin the shift; the successor programme should put adaptation at the centre, with these five as structural benchmarks carrying provincial timelines. The Fund’s leverage transformed Pakistan’s energy use by accident. It can now be used on water deliberately. Some things need capital: flood protection, climate-proofed infrastructure, livestock systems that cut methane. That is where concessional finance belongs. A country that has done the rest with its own instruments makes a far stronger case for it. Phase one happened by accident. Phase two cannot. Islamabad should design the next transformation, in water as well as power, rather than wait for the next IMF programme to force it. The first revolution cut Pakistan’s fuel bill and emissions. The second can make the country resilient.
articles.author: Ali Tauqeer Sheikh

articles.title: Exchange rate & other protections
articles.content: THERE is always something a little off when economists and other experts say that a given course of action is beneficial for industrial growth in the country, but those industries directly connected with that course of action or policy direction are silent on the matter. Normally, industry is very vocal about preserving its interests and either takes the lead in advocating its preferences, or at least responds to suggestions coming from other quarters. These days we are seeing this happen in two areas. One is the conversation around the exchange rate. All manner of articles have been written about whether the exchange rate needs to be devalued to keep exports competitive. Those advocating this are pointing to the so-called Real Effective Exchange Rate, or REER, which, they say, is overvalued, making Pakistani products expensive in export markets by comparison to our main export competitors. The REER is a tool used mainly by central bankers and academics to measure how a given country’s exchange rate is aligned with the inflation-adjusted exchange rates of its main trading partners. The way it works is simple. When the REER is 100 there is, in theory anyway, alignment between Pakistan and its trading partners in terms of how well the exchange rate reflects the costs of doing business in Pakistan versus its competitor countries. But if the REER rises above 100 it is considered overvalued, meaning the exchange rate no longer adequately reflects the rising price level within the country by comparison to its competitors, and keeping it at present-day levels will render exports non-competitive. The more the REER is above 100, the more overvalued the rupee is considered to be. And if it is below 100, then the exchange rate can be considered undervalued, meaning exporters are enjoying a premium in international markets by comparison to the cost of doing business that faces their competitors in other countries. Conditions that have historically called for an exchange rate devaluation are simply not there today. Now here is the strange thing. The REER has been above 100 for a number of months now, and is now far enough above its equilibrium level to potentially merit a devaluation. But none among the exporter community is demanding this. Not publicly anyway. All exporter associations, and other chambers around the country, are very vocal about the direction of interest rates, about the taxation burden, about electricity and gas pricing. But not a word about the exchange rate. So what to make of a situation where economists are saying the currency needs to depreciate to make exports competitive, but exporters themselves are making no such demand? Another example is with theauto policythat the government has been working on for many months now. A couple of years ago they brought customs duties down on imported vehicles, and are now moving to cut import tariffs further on other manufactured goods. Despite a few years of applying this trade policy, and now moving to codify the gradual elimination of protections in a new auto policy, the auto companies themselves are silent. Sharp objections are being raised by manufacturers of auto parts, organised under an umbrella grouping called Pakistan Auto and Auto Parts Manufacturers Association (PAAPAM), who rightly argue that large investments made in the manufacture of auto parts like vehicle glass, headlights, doors, bonnets, other body parts and lots more are at risk with this new policy. So far their objections have not prevailed over the cabinet, though they have found sympathetic ears within government. What is striking is the silence of the key stakeholders — the auto companies themselves. Why are those whose business is directly in line to be impacted by this measure not saying anything about it, at least publicly? The answer is a little obvious: the proposed measure does not adversely impact their interests. The exporters are not asking for a devaluation and auto makers are not asking for the return of the protections behind which they grew up, because their business is not going to be as adversely or favourably impacted by the proposed measures as theory might tell us. The auto part manufacturers are a different story. They cannot sell their parts to anybody else other than the big auto makers for whom they have been vendors for many years now. Changing that would require a deep process of retooling their plant, and figuring out where auto volumes are sufficiently mature to merit retooling the plant and producing parts at industrial scale. Given that the auto industry is in the middle of shifting to electric vehicles anyway, such a process of obsolescence and adaptation to a changing market reality is perhaps coming anyway, regardless of how much protection the government extends to legacy manufacturers. Regarding the exchange rate, policymakers in Pakistan have never paid much mind to the REER in deciding the level they want for the rate. The level is usually decided more with rupee cost of external debt servicing requirements in mind, first and foremost. Adjustments to the exchange rate always come when their hand is forced by market reality, which means devaluations come when the State Bank’s liquid reserves fall below the level required to keep rampant dollarisation in check. Never have they based exchange rate decisions on export competitiveness and there is no reason to suppose they are about to change now. Conditions that have historically called for an exchange rate devaluation are simply not there today. First, there is an abundant supply of dollars by comparison to the supply of rupees in the market, and the position is only improving. Second, there is no flight into the dollar. Third, the interbank market is virtually shut, with banks told (through silent channels) to finance their clients’ import requirements from their own inflows, while the State Bank aggressively buys these inflows at a steadily appreciating rate, to fuel its own thirst for dollars. Under these conditions, the REER is about as relevant as the daily weather forecast. There will be no devaluation in the near future, not until their hand is forced by market reality. The writer is a business and economy journalist.
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: La nuora Italiana
articles.content: THREE female imports symbolise India: London-born Annie Besant, who became the president of the Indian National Congress in 1917; Gonxha Agnes (later Mother Teresa) who received India’s third Nobel Prize in 1979 for the succour she gave to the dying in Kolkata; and Sonia Gandhi (an Italian) who became the longest-serving president of the INC (1998-2017, 2019-2022). Sonia came to India in January 1968 to marry Rajiv (Mrs Indira Gandhi’s eldest son). They wanted nothing more than an unobtrusive life together — he as a commercial airline pilot, she a casalinga or homemaker. However, neither could escape their destiny, nor death which stalked them. Their first son died soon after birth. Rajiv’s younger brother Sanjay plummeted to his death performing aerial stunts over Delhi. Their mother was assassinated in 1984. And Rajiv fell victim to an LTTE suicide bomber in 1991. Sonia has survived, to tell her own story, and theirs. Sonia Gandhi’s memoirs — Belonging: a Journey of Love (2026) — are a rosary of reminiscences. One section marks her minority as a middle-class Italian Catholic; the second, her assimilation into the Nehru-Gandhi dynasty; and the third, her powerful widowhood. Sonia Gandhi’s memoirs are a rosary of reminiscences. Her marriage to Rajiv alienated her conservative father. He half-expected it to fail, absenting himself from the wedding with “a brief, cold” note: ‘‘Remember that the door of this house will always be open for you.’’ Amongst Sonia’s in-laws, Mrs Gandhi remained her closest ally, and for a while Rajiv’s younger brother Sanjay. Sonia noticed, though, a simmering tension between the siblings. Sanjay “was intensely competitive — he just had to know more and do better”. Rajiv stayed out of politics while Sanjay used his position as his mother’s favourite to influence her with insidious, often dangerous advice. The situation in Mrs Gandhi’s joint family household deteriorated after Sanjay’s marriage to Maneka Anand, a Punjabi Sikh. Mrs Gandhi thought the immature Maneka too ambitious by half, the half being her pushy mother Amardeep Kaur. Tensions overflowed after Mrs Gandhi’s defeat in the 1977 elections, when the family were compressed into a four-bedroom house at 12 Willingdon Crescent (lent to them by Yunus Khan). They had to share transport, cut back on staff. They became ‘hypersensitive’. Rajiv held Sanjay responsible for their mother’s humiliating ouster. During one fracas, Rajiv said vehemently, “I cannot forgive you, Sanjay — you have brought Ma to this pass.” Mrs Gandhi, ‘upset and agitated’, assented: “What Rajiv said is true, Sanjay! How many times you gave orders without my knowledge.’’ Ludicrously, according to Sonia, the only real “flare-up between the brothers” occurred after Sanjay’s wolfhound savaged Rajiv’s meeker dog Zabul. On Oct 31, 1984, Sonia cradled a dying Indira Gandhi in her lap during the unconscionably long journey to the hospital in an Ambassador car. Surprisingly, there was no ambulance on duty at PM’s house. Sonia tried desperately to prevent Rajiv from inheriting the premiership: “You must say no — for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you”. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.” And they did, in May 1991. Cruelly widowed, Sonia Gandhi could have deflected destiny and returned to Italy. Why did she choose to stay on? Had Mrs Gandhi trained her for the prime ministership? No more than Pandit Nehru had tutored Indira. Mrs Gandhi explained her own self-tutoring: “You come to a river in the middle of a forest and there is a river across the way [.] Unless of your own accord, you learn how to swim, you will have to turn back, or die.” Sonia confesses to being tormented at seeing the “all-inclusive ethos” of the Congress Party being assailed by “the relentless advance of the communal [BJP] forces”. In a move one expected to read in Narendra Modi’s memoirs, she turned to the Bhagavad Gita for guidance. In January 1997, aided by a ‘Shastri-ji’, she began reading the Gita in translation. After a year of studious meditation, she felt inspired by Krishna’s message in the Gita: “Perform your dharma [duty] without regard for the fruit of your action”. Despite the objections of her children, she conceded to the demands of the headless Congress. Like Annie Besant and Mother Teresa before her, she felt compelled to answer India’s call to duty. Canvassing tirelessly, Sonia Gandhi led the Congress to victory in 2004 and 2009. During those 10 years, she ill-used Dr Manmohan Singh as her stringless PM puppet. Now in opposition, she concedes that PM Modi and she have little in common: he is a product of an antediluvian RSS, leapfrogging into the future; she the legatee of Nehru’s sentimental secularism. She expects young India to allow Rahul and Priyanka to fulfil their dynastic destiny.
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: Arab blood
articles.content: TO shed Arab blood, it is not necessary for the ‘shedder’ to be a non-Arab. Thousands, for example, have died in Yemen, while millions have been displaced due to the conflict. Well, it is war — and in the Middle East. Usually, a war in the Middle East meant a slaughter between Israel and the Arabs. There were exceptions, like Saddam Hussein’s Kuwait misadventure, and his attack on Iran, when Imam Khomeini was at the peak of his power. This time it is war among the Arabs with no holds barred. Fuming with rage, the 90-year-old Saudi monarch, King Salman, has dubbed the Houthis a “terrorist militia” and vowed retaliation. The anger was expected, because Houthi strikes on such a sensitive institution as Riyadh’s international airport have killed a number of people. More regretfully, any possibility that the war may not spread disappeared when US President Donald Trump had said, after the Riyadh airport attack last month, that his country could join Saudi attacks on the Houthis. Arabs are mere spectators of the international drama. Lack of unity doesn’t necessarily mean enmity. If the Arabs cannot unite, the least they can do is not make a spectacle of their disunity and invite the world’s contempt by talking about liberating Palestine and Jerusalem. Unity, we must know, is a precursor to thought and action. Some key Arab governments have expressed interest in joining the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed on Aug 7 this year, while Iran and the Houthis are allies. The two defence alliances are confrontational in spirit. A look at numerous recent news reports gives a fairly good idea of how so many Arab governments and factions are at war with each other. So read on: “In a lightning offensive … the Houthis seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is vital to Saudi crude exports. “Pakistan also joined the Muslim world in condemning the alleged Houthi attacks on holy cities in Saudi Arabia and called for urgent de-escalation in Yemen. “Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry condemned the purported targeting of Makkah as a “cowardly terrorist attack,” and reaffirmed the kingdom’s right to “defend the security of the two holy mosques, the pilgrims, and the entire Saudi territory”. “A Houthi politburo member dismissed the accusation as “a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone”. “The Houthis also claimed Saudi warplanes launched 40 airstrikes … targeting the provinces of Taiz, Marib, and Hodeidah. “Pakistan’s approach to the conflict seems to be to seek an end to hostilities rather than become part of an expanding military confrontation. “These developments must be seen against the background of Pakistan’s growing defence commitments to Saudi Arabia, especially the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) and the recently signed Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. “In September last year, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a treaty under which aggression against either country is to be treated as aggression against both. “Pakistan already maintains military personnel and defence assets in Saudi Arabia, with the two countries having long-standing military cooperation that predates SMDA.” The more you read, the more you realise how divided the Muslim world is and how this internal Saracenic rivalry in the world of Islam is the greatest asset others have. While talking of Arab unity and joint defence agreement, let us note that the United Arab Emirates, a major Arab oil power, has quit both OPEC and OPEC+, of which it has been a member for 60 years. It was hardly on speaking terms with Saudi Arabia because of differences over a number of issues, though mat-ters have improved recently. The UAE supports Yemen’s Southern Transitional Council (STC). It made a major geopolitical mistake when it sent troops into eastern Yemen in support of the STC near Saudi borders. This alarmed Riyadh, which rushed its troops, bombed STC targets and forced a UAE withdrawal. By any standard it was a Saudi victory and an Emirati humiliation. Look at the language the Houthis and the Saudis are using. To talk of Arab, much less Muslim, unity is to invite the world’s contempt. Arabs are mere spectators of the international drama unfolding around them. Despite having all the money in the world, not one Arab country has internationally recognised institutes of science and technology. There are hundreds of thousands of Arab students in Europe and America, but they have chosen to live as migrants instead of achieving fame as scholars and inventors. This is the price they are paying for ignoring science and technology. The writer is Dawn’s External Ombudsman and an author.
articles.author: Muhammad Ali Siddiqi

articles.title: Hardening lines
articles.content: THE battle lines are being drawn over the creation of new provinces, as the two main partners in the ruling coalition experience a democratic reawakening. Both have recently taken to extolling the virtues of democracy — but each with their own spin. On one side, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari istaking a hard standagainst a division of the provinces “imposed by force”. He has warned it might lead to bloodshed. As an alternative, he is pushing the idea of a political reset, which would entail recognising and respecting the mandate given to opposition parties, especially the PTI. On the other side, various government ministers, mostly from the PML-N, arelecturinganyone who will listen on the merits of a public referendum. Though the controversies that followed the general elections are yet to be resolved, they are arguing, rather earnestly, that holding a nationwide referendum on new provinces is the fairest way forward. Mr Bhutto-Zardari made an astute observation in his Tuesday speech at the Karachi Press Club: “In our history, a referendum has always been carried out for an undemocratic act and never a democratic one.” More jarring was his revelation that “up until today, neither the prime minister nor a single member of the cabinet has brought up the issue [of new provinces] with the president of Pakistan or me”. What is one to make of this, considering that several members of the federal cabinet, including the ministers of interior, defence and information, have been making rather forceful public statements on the topic? It suggests the issue is being litigated in the media rather than discussed among the political leadership. Mr Bhutto-Zardari seemed frustrated with the prime minister’s silence when his ministers seem eager to discuss it. It is also strange that the president, too, has not weighed in. Perhaps the elders in both parties, the president among them, are testing the waters by letting Mr Bhutto-Zardari and second-tier ministers lead the conversation for now. But the issue will be taken up in some form sooner rather than later, and they cannot wait until the eleventh hour to make their official positions known. The administrative reconfiguration of an entire country — one that ranks among the most populous in the world — is no ordinary task. It is not merely a question of drawing lines on a map: nearly every branch of the state will need to be restructured around the new configuration, and this cannot be achieved through fiat. The Constitution already sets out the route: altering a province’s limits requires a constitutional amendment backed by two-thirds of that province’s assembly. Rather than trading referendums for ultimatums, the political leadership should take the question to parliament and the provincial assemblies, and build consensus there.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Structural reforms
articles.content: THE country’s improving macroeconomic health offers little hope when growth remains too weak to create enough jobs or improve living standards. The State Bank’s latest annual report makes this contradiction difficult to ignore. It argues that structural reforms are essential for putting the economy on a sustainable high-growth path. The figures underline the scale of the problem. The SBP has correctly identified premature deindustrialisation, weak investment, inadequate skills and widespread informal employment as major constraints. These problems have accumulated over decades of inconsistent economic policies. The state’s reform priorities must therefore address the reasons businesses hesitate to invest and expand. Infrastructure gaps require attention. Tax administration needs simplification, with a broader tax base. Businesses also need predictable regulations and consistent policies. Repeated policy reversals have made long-term planning difficult for domestic and foreign investors alike. The domestic labour market presents an equally serious challenge. While overall unemployment has risen to 7.2pc in 2025 from 5.7pc in 2018, low female workforce participation keeps a substantial share of potential workers outside productive economic activity. High youth unemployment reflects weaknesses in education and vocational training. Universities and technical institutions must develop skills that employers actually need. The agricultural sector needs modern irrigation, better technology and climate-resilient practices. However, the most important lesson from the SBP report concerns policy continuity. Structural reforms cannot succeed through isolated announcements or short-lived initiatives. They require political commitment across successive governments. Every change in administration should not bring another round of economic experimentation. The government must recognise that sustainable growth requires a stronger productive base. Without consistent investment, industrial expansion, better skills and higher productivity, economic stability will remain vulnerable. The real test of reform will be whether it creates productive jobs and raises household incomes.
articles.author: Editorial
